passages.passage_text: Group polarization is the tendency for group discussion to strengthen the position members held beforehand. Researchers recruited 120 undergraduates and formed 24 five-person groups, each made up of members whose private ratings of a risky financial option were similar. Each participant first rated, on a scale from 1 (never) to 9 (definitely), willingness to take the option. Twelve groups (discussion condition) then talked for 15 minutes about whether the option was wise. The other 12 groups (control condition) sat in the same room for 15 minutes working on unrelated puzzles without talking. Everyone then rated the option again, privately. A group was classed as risk-leaning if its mean first rating exceeded 5 and cautious-leaning if it was below 5. Coders also tallied arguments voiced in the discussion groups: 78% of arguments in risk-leaning groups favored the option, and 74% of arguments in cautious-leaning groups opposed it. Table 1 and Figure 1 show group-level means.
passages.table_data:
| Condition | Initial lean | Groups (n) | Before mean | After mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discussion | Risk-leaning | 6 | 6.2 | 7.4 |
| Discussion | Cautious-leaning | 6 | 3.8 | 2.7 |
| Control | Risk-leaning | 6 | 6.1 | 6.2 |
| Control | Cautious-leaning | 6 | 3.9 | 3.9 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Mean willingness to take the risky option

questions.stem: Which result in Table 1 best demonstrates group polarization?

options.A: Both kinds of discussion group moved toward the scale midpoint after talking, reflecting a compromise among members.
options.B: Discussion groups ended farther from the scale midpoint in the direction of their initial lean, whereas control groups barely changed.
options.C: Every group, including those that never talked, became more extreme after 15 minutes, so the change reflects time alone.
options.D: After discussion, risk-leaning and cautious-leaning groups became more similar to each other than they had been before.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Risk-leaning discussion groups rose from 6.2 to 7.4 and cautious-leaning discussion groups fell from 3.8 to 2.7, both moving away from 5, while controls stayed essentially flat. Why the others are wrong: A) Movement toward 5 would indicate convergence; the discussion means moved away from 5 in both subgroups. C) Control groups changed by 0.1 point or less, so time and repeated rating did not produce the shifts. D) The gap between lean types widened (about 2.4 points before, 4.7 after), so the groups became less similar.
questions.trap: Assuming that any change after discussion is a compromise toward the middle, instead of checking the direction of each group's shift.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the control condition in this study?

options.A: To guarantee that participants in the discussion condition had been assigned to groups of the same size as the other condition.
options.B: To supply the coded arguments that allowed researchers to estimate how persuasive each position was in the discussion groups.
options.C: To show that the shifts seen in the discussion groups were not produced merely by the passage of time and rating the option twice.
options.D: To remove demand characteristics entirely, since control participants cannot guess the hypothesis being tested by the researchers.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Control groups had the same delay, setting, and repeated rating but no discussion, so any difference from the discussion groups can be attributed to talking. Why the others are wrong: A) Group sizes were fixed at five in both conditions by design; the control does not serve this function. B) Only the discussion groups produced arguments to code; control groups did not talk. D) Control participants can still form guesses about the study, so demand characteristics are not eliminated.
questions.trap: Treating a control group as a way to remove every bias rather than as a baseline for the manipulated variable.

questions.stem: Which additional finding would favor the persuasive-arguments explanation of polarization over a social-comparison explanation?

options.A: Polarization occurred only when members learned how their own ratings compared with the ratings of the other group members.
options.B: Groups polarized even when members heard one another's arguments but never learned each other's ratings.
options.C: Polarization was larger in groups whose members said they liked and wanted to impress one another.
options.D: Polarization vanished when members were told the group's average rating before they spoke.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) If arguments alone, without information about others' positions, produce a shift, then exposure to novel arguments rather than comparison with others is the driver. Why the others are wrong: A) This outcome depends on seeing others' ratings, which is what a social-comparison account predicts. C) Stronger effects with greater liking and impression management fit a social-comparison account. D) Disappearance when only the average is known would suggest that comparison information, not arguments, matters.
questions.trap: Choosing a result that fits both explanations rather than one that separates them.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers treat the 12 groups per condition, rather than the 60 individuals, as the units of analysis?

options.A: Ratings on a 9-point scale are too coarse to be compared across individual participants in a meaningful way.
options.B: Averaging within groups removes the influence of initial lean, which would otherwise hide the effect of discussion.
options.C: After discussion, members influenced one another, so their ratings are not independent observations.
options.D: Group means vary more than individual ratings, which lowers the risk of a Type I error in the comparison.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Independence of observations is a core assumption of standard tests; using individuals would inflate the effective sample size and exaggerate significance. Why the others are wrong: A) Scale coarseness is not the issue; individual ratings could still be analyzed if they were independent. B) Initial lean was used to classify groups and is still visible in the means, so it is not removed. D) Group means actually vary less than individual scores, and the choice is about independence, not Type I error control per se.
questions.trap: Counting the 120 participants as 120 independent data points even though discussion makes group members' responses dependent.

questions.stem: What was the average shift in the direction of initial lean across the two discussion subgroups?

options.A: 0.05 points
options.B: 2.30 points
options.C: 0.58 points
options.D: 1.15 points

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Risk-leaning groups moved +1.2 in their lean direction and cautious-leaning groups moved 1.1 in theirs, so the average is (1.2 + 1.1) / 2 = 1.15. Why the others are wrong: A) Subtracting the signed changes (+1.2 and -1.1) cancels the shifts and ignores their direction relative to lean. B) Adding the two shifts gives the total, not the average. C) Dividing the total by four rather than by two halves the correct average again.
questions.trap: Averaging signed changes (+1.2 and -1.1), which cancels two shifts that are both movements toward greater extremity.

passages.passage_text: The overjustification effect holds that rewarding an activity people already enjoy can reduce later interest in it. Researchers observed 90 children, ages 4 and 5, during one week of free play with markers and paper, and enrolled children who chose to draw for a substantial share of the time. A week later, children were randomly assigned to three conditions (n = 30 each). In the expected-reward condition, children were told before drawing that they would earn a certificate. In the unexpected-reward condition, children drew with no mention of a prize and were given a certificate afterward. In the no-reward condition, children drew and received nothing. Two weeks after that session, observers who did not know the conditions recorded the percentage of free-play time each child spent drawing. Table 1 lists condition means, with standard deviations in parentheses. Children whose parents had not consented to observation were not enrolled, and all children were treated kindly and given a small gift at the end of the study regardless of condition. Sessions took place in the same classroom with the same materials, and an adult stayed nearby in every session.
passages.table_data:
| Condition | Baseline drawing time (%) | Follow-up drawing time (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Expected reward | 61 (14) | 34 (12) |
| Unexpected reward | 63 (13) | 59 (12) |
| No reward | 62 (15) | 60 (13) |

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the drop in drawing time in the expected-reward group?

options.A: Children inferred that they had drawn for the certificate, which weakened their view of drawing as something they did because they enjoyed it.
options.B: Children felt dissonance about being paid too little for drawing and so changed their attitude toward the activity.
options.C: Children observed peers who stopped drawing after earning certificates and imitated that behavior during later free play.
options.D: Repeated exposure to the markers caused habituation, so the children stopped responding to the drawing materials.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This is the self-perception and overjustification account: a salient external reward becomes the perceived cause of the behavior, undermining intrinsic motivation. Why the others are wrong: B) A small reward producing dissonance would predict more, not less, liking; the reward here was framed as a prize, and drawing time fell. C) There was no peer modeling in the design; children drew individually. D) Habituation would also have affected the unexpected-reward and no-reward groups, whose drawing time stayed near baseline.
questions.trap: Reaching for a familiar concept (imitation or habituation) without checking whether the design could produce it in only one group.

questions.stem: What is the main reason the study included an unexpected-reward group?

options.A: To see whether receiving a reward without expecting it lowers later interest.
options.B: To check that children in all three groups drew for equal amounts of time at baseline.
options.C: To serve as a placebo condition in which children cannot tell that they are being observed.
options.D: To determine whether the observers could correctly guess which condition each child had been in.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The only difference between the expected-reward and unexpected-reward groups is whether the reward was anticipated while drawing, isolating expectation as the key factor. Why the others are wrong: B) Baseline equivalence is checked with the baseline column, not with this extra group. C) A placebo group is not defined by hidden observation, and observation was equal across groups anyway. D) Observers were meant to be unaware of conditions; guessing accuracy was not the purpose.
questions.trap: Confusing a comparison group that isolates one variable with a baseline or blinding check.

questions.stem: By what percentage did mean drawing time decrease from baseline to follow-up in the expected-reward group?

options.B: About 44%

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The drop was 61 - 34 = 27 percentage points, and 27 / 61 is about 0.44, or 44% of the baseline value. Why the others are wrong: A) 27 is the absolute decrease in percentage points, not the percent decrease relative to baseline. C) 34 / 61 is about 56%, which is the share of baseline time remaining rather than the share lost. D) 27 / 34 is about 79%, which wrongly uses the follow-up value as the denominator.
questions.trap: Reporting the point difference (27) as a percent decrease, or dividing by the follow-up value instead of the baseline.

questions.stem: Which situation is most consistent with the overjustification effect?

options.A: A teenager who loved reading for fun joins a program that pays her for each book, then reads less on her own once the program ends.
options.B: A worker pays closer attention to details while a quarterly bonus is available, and relaxes when it is not offered.
options.C: A student given a surprise gift after a strong exam continues to study at the same rate as before.
options.D: A dog trained with treats sits reliably when a treat is visible but ignores the command when none is shown.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) An already enjoyed activity, a contingent expected reward, and a later decline in voluntary engagement is the pattern the effect describes. Why the others are wrong: B) Effort that tracks an available bonus shows ordinary extrinsic motivation, not erosion of an existing intrinsic interest. C) An unexpected gift is not predicted to change interest, matching the unexpected-reward group. D) This is learned dependence on a reinforcer, not a loss of intrinsic interest in the activity.
questions.trap: Picking any example involving rewards without requiring prior intrinsic interest and a later drop after the reward.

passages.passage_text: Social comparison theory proposes that people evaluate themselves by comparing their abilities and outcomes with those of others. Eighty college students were told that a study concerned problem-solving styles. Each completed a short creativity test and then waited for results in a room with another 'participant' who was actually a trained confederate. The confederate revealed a score that was either better (upward) or worse (downward) than the participant's own, and was presented as either a student in the same major (similar) or in an unrelated major (dissimilar). A fifth group waited alone (control). Sixteen participants were randomly assigned to each of the five conditions. Afterward, all completed a 0 to 100 state self-esteem scale. Table 1 lists the results, and Figure 1 plots the four comparison conditions. The confederates followed a written script, wore similar clothing, and were rotated across conditions so that no single confederate was linked to one condition. Participants were fully informed about the study only after the final questionnaire.
passages.table_data:
| Condition | n | Mean self-esteem | SD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upward, similar | 16 | 58 | 12 |
| Upward, dissimilar | 16 | 68 | 12 |
| Downward, similar | 16 | 76 | 12 |
| Downward, dissimilar | 16 | 71 | 12 |
| Control | 16 | 70 | 12 |

graph.title: Figure 1. State self-esteem by comparison direction and target similarity

questions.stem: Which outcome in Table 1 is consistent with social comparison theory?

options.A: Downward comparison with a dissimilar student produced lower self-esteem than the control condition.
options.B: Upward comparison with a dissimilar student produced higher self-esteem than the control condition.
options.C: Upward comparison with a similar student produced lower self-esteem than the control condition.
options.D: The control group showed higher self-esteem than every group that made a comparison.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Falling behind a comparable other (58 versus 70 in control) lowers self-evaluation, as the theory predicts. Why the others are wrong: A) The downward dissimilar mean (71) was slightly above control (70), not below it. B) The upward dissimilar mean (68) was below control (70), not above it. D) Both downward conditions (76 and 71) exceeded the control mean of 70.
questions.trap: Assuming control must be the highest group, or ignoring which direction each comparison moved self-esteem relative to control.

questions.stem: Why might upward comparison with a dissimilar student lower self-esteem less than upward comparison with a similar student?

options.A: Dissimilar students are likely to be perceived as less intelligent, which makes the participant feel more capable by contrast.
options.B: Participants in the dissimilar conditions had higher self-esteem before the study, so they had more to lose from the comparison.
options.C: Dissimilar targets reduce the effect of the confederate's score because participants cannot hear what the confederate says.
options.D: A dissimilar person is a less relevant standard, so that person's better performance says less about the participant's own ability.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Comparison matters most when the target is similar on relevant attributes; a different-major peer offers less diagnostic information about one's own standing. Why the others are wrong: A) The mechanism is relevance of the standard, not a belief that the other student is less intelligent. B) Random assignment makes pre-existing self-esteem equal across conditions on average. C) Both conditions heard the same kind of score disclosure; hearing was not manipulated.
questions.trap: Inventing a baseline difference between groups despite random assignment.

questions.stem: Which statement about Figure 1 describes an interaction between comparison direction and similarity?

options.A: Both upward and downward comparisons lower self-esteem when the target is similar to the participant.
options.B: Self-esteem is higher in the dissimilar conditions regardless of whether the comparison is upward or downward.
options.C: The effect of target similarity runs in opposite directions for upward and downward comparisons.
options.D: Upward and downward lines are parallel, showing that direction has an effect independent of similarity.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Upward comparison scored higher with dissimilar targets (68 versus 58), but downward comparison scored lower with dissimilar targets (71 versus 76), so the lines cross. Why the others are wrong: A) Downward comparison with a similar target gave the highest self-esteem (76), not a lowered score. B) Downward dissimilar (71) was below downward similar (76), so the statement fails for downward comparisons. D) The lines are not parallel: they slope in opposite directions and cross.
questions.trap: Calling any two effects an interaction instead of checking whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

questions.stem: Because participants were deceived about the purpose of the study, what is the most important ethical step after data collection?

options.A: Destroying all data from participants in the upward-comparison conditions so that the lowered scores cannot be used.
options.B: Excluding participants who suspected the confederate from being told the true purpose of the study.
options.C: Debriefing participants about the deception and addressing any lowered self-esteem.
options.D: Offering the control participants the opportunity to repeat the study in a comparison condition.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Deception is acceptable only when needed and when participants are fully informed afterward and any distress is mitigated. Why the others are wrong: A) Data are not discarded because they are unflattering; the issue is participant welfare. B) All participants, including those who suspected the confederate, are owed an explanation. D) Offering a repeat does not address the deception or any harm already experienced.
questions.trap: Confusing data quality procedures with obligations to the participants after deception.

questions.stem: Using the standard error of the mean, which interval best approximates the 95% confidence interval for the upward-similar group?
questions.explanation: Correct: C) SE = SD / square root of n = 12 / 4 = 3, and 58 plus or minus about 2 SE (6 points) gives 52 to 64, which excludes the control mean of 70. Why the others are wrong: A) 46 to 70 is the mean plus or minus 1 SD (12), the spread of individual scores rather than the uncertainty of the mean; it wrongly reaches the control mean. B) 55 to 61 uses only 1 SE on each side, a roughly 68% interval. D) 56 to 60 corresponds to about 0.7 SE and is too narrow for a 95% interval.
questions.trap: Using the standard deviation in place of the standard error, which widens the interval and makes the group look indistinguishable from control.

passages.passage_text: Researchers tested whether teacher expectations influence student performance. At the start of the school year, teachers in 24 elementary classrooms (eight each in grades 1, 3, and 5) were told that a new test had identified about one in five students as 'bloomers' who were likely to show unusual intellectual growth. In fact, the bloomers had been chosen by lottery, and the test had not been scored. Eight months later, testers who did not know which students had been labeled gave an alternate form of the same ability test. Observers also recorded that teachers gave labeled first graders more feedback and more challenging assignments than their classmates. Table 1 shows the mean gain in test score (points) for labeled and unlabeled students. The classrooms came from three schools serving similar neighborhoods. Within each classroom, labeled students were chosen by lottery regardless of their earlier performance, and teachers were asked not to discuss the labels with students or parents.
passages.table_data:
| Grade | Labeled students (n) | Labeled mean gain | Unlabeled students (n) | Unlabeled mean gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 34 | 12.8 | 146 | 7.0 |
| 3 | 38 | 6.1 | 152 | 5.4 |
| 5 | 36 | 5.2 | 144 | 4.9 |

questions.stem: Why does the random selection of 'bloomers' allow the researchers to attribute gain differences to the label?

options.A: Random selection ensures that testers cannot tell which students were labeled when they score the tests.
options.B: Random selection guarantees that teachers treat labeled and unlabeled students in the same way during the year.
options.C: Random selection increases the number of labeled students, which gives the study greater statistical power.
options.D: Random selection makes labeled and unlabeled students similar in ability at the start, so the label is the only systematic difference.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Because the lottery is unrelated to ability, preexisting differences should balance out on average, supporting a causal claim about the label. Why the others are wrong: A) Hiding labels from testers was a separate step; random selection does not blind anyone. B) Teachers evidently did not treat students alike; observers saw more feedback for labeled first graders. C) The labeled fraction was fixed at about one in five; randomization does not enlarge it.
questions.trap: Mixing up random assignment, which equates groups, with blinding, which prevents biased measurement.

questions.stem: Why was it important that the testers did not know which students had been labeled?

options.A: So that labeled students would not realize they had been selected and change their own behavior.
options.B: So that the testers could be matched to classrooms with the same number of labeled students.
options.C: So that their own expectations could not influence how they administered or scored the tests.
options.D: So that the alternate test form would be certain to measure the same ability as the original form.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Observer or experimenter bias is itself an expectancy effect; blinding testers prevents it from contaminating the outcome measure. Why the others are wrong: A) Student awareness is a different concern; the students were never told about the labels. B) Matching testers to classrooms has nothing to do with blinding. D) Test-form equivalence is a property of the test, not of tester knowledge.
questions.trap: Treating blinding as a way to hide information from participants rather than from the people who measure outcomes.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The advantage of labeled students was largest in grade 1 and was nearly absent by grade 5.
options.B: The new test accurately identified students who were about to show unusual intellectual growth.
options.C: Teachers in grades 3 and 5 ignored the labels entirely and treated all students identically.
options.D: Unlabeled first graders showed no improvement in test scores over the eight months.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The labeled-minus-unlabeled gap was 5.8 points in grade 1, 0.7 in grade 3, and 0.3 in grade 5. Why the others are wrong: B) The labels came from a lottery and the test was never scored, so it could not have predicted anything. C) A small gap does not show that teachers ignored labels; the table has no behavioral data for those grades. D) Unlabeled first graders gained 7.0 points, so they did improve.
questions.trap: Overstating a pattern in the data into a claim about teacher behavior or test accuracy that the table cannot support.

questions.stem: Labeled first graders received more feedback and harder assignments and then gained more. Which concept does this sequence best illustrate?

options.A: The fundamental attribution error, in which observers explain students' performance by their dispositions rather than the situation.
options.B: The halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments about unrelated traits of the same student.
options.C: Confirmation bias in scoring, in which testers interpret ambiguous answers to fit what they expect.
options.D: A self-fulfilling prophecy, in which an initially false expectation leads to behavior that makes it come true.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Teachers' expectations altered their treatment of students, which in turn produced the improvement the label had predicted. Why the others are wrong: A) The fundamental attribution error concerns explaining behavior, not expectations that change outcomes. B) The halo effect is about generalizing one trait; the key element here is behavior that confirms the label. C) Testers were blind to labels, so biased scoring cannot account for the result.
questions.trap: Choosing a social-cognition bias that describes a judgment rather than the loop from expectation to behavior to outcome.

passages.passage_text: To study how proximity affects friendship formation, researchers followed 500 first-year students who were randomly assigned to rooms along dormitory hallways. At the end of the first term, each student named close friends among hallmates. Researchers then coded pairs of hallmates as adjacent (rooms next to each other) or far (four or more doors apart), and as high or low in attitude similarity based on a questionnaire completed at orientation, before rooms were assigned. Table 1 gives the percentage of pairs in which at least one student named the other as a close friend, for the 1,000 pairs that were either adjacent or far apart. Figure 1 adds pairs two and three doors apart and shows friendship rates for all pairs by distance in doors. Students could request a room change after the first week, but fewer than 5% did so, and requests were not included in the analysis. Friendship reports were collected privately, and students did not see one another's answers.
passages.table_data:
| Pair type | Pairs (n) | Friends (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Adjacent, high similarity | 200 | 38 |
| Adjacent, low similarity | 300 | 17 |
| Far, high similarity | 150 | 12 |
| Far, low similarity | 350 | 4 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Friendship rate by distance between rooms
graph.x_label: Distance between rooms (doors apart; 4 = four or more)

questions.stem: Which principle best explains why friendship rates decline with distance in Figure 1?

options.A: Cognitive dissonance, in which people change their attitudes after acting against them.
options.B: The mere exposure effect, in which repeated contact increases familiarity and liking.
options.C: The bystander effect, in which the presence of others reduces each person's willingness to act.
options.D: Reciprocity of liking, in which people dislike anyone who does not first express interest in them.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Closer neighbors encounter each other more often, and repeated exposure tends to raise liking, which makes friendships more likely. Why the others are wrong: A) Dissonance is about conflict between attitudes and behavior and does not predict declining friendship with distance. C) The bystander effect concerns helping in emergencies. D) Reciprocal liking can help friendships form but does not explain why distance matters.
questions.trap: Selecting a well-known social psychology effect that does not address how frequency of contact changes attraction.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of randomly assigning students to rooms?

options.A: It guarantees that every pair of hallmates would have the same attitude similarity.
options.B: It ensures that friendships formed in the dormitory are stronger than those formed elsewhere.
options.C: It rules out the possibility that students chose to live near people they already liked.
options.D: It makes the sample of 500 students representative of all first-year students nationwide.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Without random assignment, self-selection of neighbors could create the proximity-friendship link, so random assignment supports a causal reading of proximity. Why the others are wrong: A) Random assignment of rooms does not equalize similarity between pairs; similarity varied across pairs. B) Nothing about room assignment tells us about friendships formed elsewhere. D) Representativeness depends on how students were sampled, not on room assignment.
questions.trap: Confusing random assignment, which supports internal validity, with random sampling, which supports generalization.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is NOT justified by the study?

options.A: Pairs of adjacent hallmates were more likely to be friends than pairs far apart.
options.B: Attitude similarity causes friendship, because similarity was measured, not manipulated, and friends may become alike over time.
options.C: Far pairs with high similarity were more likely to be friends than far pairs with low similarity.
options.D: Friendship rates declined as the distance between rooms increased.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Similarity was an observed characteristic; only room placement was randomized, so a causal claim about similarity is unsupported. Why the others are wrong: A) Adjacent pairs showed 38% and 17% friendship against 12% and 4% for far pairs, so this is justified. C) Far pairs with high similarity (12%) exceeded far pairs with low similarity (4%), so this is justified. D) Figure 1 shows a steady decline across the four distance categories, so this is justified.
questions.trap: Treating a correlational association between measured similarity and friendship as causal because the rest of the design was experimental.

questions.stem: What percentage of all 500 adjacent pairs were friends?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) Friends among adjacent pairs = 0.38(200) + 0.17(300) = 76 + 51 = 127, and 127 / 500 = 25.4%, which is the value plotted at 1 door in Figure 1. Why the others are wrong: A) 27.5% is the simple average of 38% and 17%, which ignores that there are more low-similarity pairs. C) 21.2% does not follow from weighting the two adjacent percentages by their numbers of pairs. D) 30.5% overweights the high-similarity pairs and does not match the table.
questions.trap: Averaging the two percentages without weighting by the number of pairs in each group.

questions.stem: Which statement about the effect of proximity is supported by Table 1?

options.A: Proximity was associated with friendship only among pairs that were high in attitude similarity.
options.B: Far pairs with high similarity were more likely to be friends than adjacent pairs with low similarity.
options.C: Similarity was associated with friendship only among pairs that were adjacent.
options.D: Proximity went with higher friendship rates at both similarity levels.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Adjacent pairs exceeded far pairs in both similarity levels (38 versus 12 and 17 versus 4). Why the others are wrong: A) Among low-similarity pairs, adjacent pairs (17%) also exceeded far pairs (4%). B) Far high-similarity pairs were 12%, below adjacent low-similarity pairs at 17%. C) Among far pairs, high similarity (12%) still exceeded low similarity (4%).
questions.trap: Inferring that an effect is limited to one subgroup after comparing only one pair of cells in the table.

passages.passage_text: Sociologists distinguish strong ties, close relationships maintained through frequent contact, from weak ties, acquaintances seen rarely. A researcher surveyed 400 workers who had started a new job within the previous year. Of these, 250 learned about the job through a personal contact; the others used advertisements or agencies. Contacts seen at least twice a week were coded as strong ties, and contacts seen once a year or less as weak ties. For each contact-based lead, respondents also reported whether the information was new, meaning that no one in their close circle knew of the opening. Respondents reported an average of 12 strong ties and 120 weak ties. Table 1 summarizes the 250 contact-based hires. Respondents were drawn from a random sample of employers in one region, and interviews were conducted by phone with trained interviewers. Industries and job levels were similar for strong-tie and weak-tie hires, according to the researcher.
passages.table_data:
| Tie type | Hires (n) | Leads that were new (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Strong tie | 100 | 20 |
| Weak tie | 150 | 60 |

questions.stem: Why would weak ties tend to supply new information about job openings?

options.A: Acquaintances belong to social circles that do not overlap with the respondent's close friends, so they hear different things.
options.B: Acquaintances have more formal authority over hiring decisions than friends or relatives do.
options.C: Strong ties are less trustworthy and therefore withhold information about openings from respondents.
options.D: People tell acquaintances more about their own lives, so weak ties know more about the respondent.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Weak ties act as bridges between otherwise separate networks (bridging social capital), carrying non-redundant information. Why the others are wrong: B) Nothing in the study suggests weak ties hold more hiring power. C) Strong ties are typically more trusted; their information is simply more redundant. D) Weak ties by definition know less about the respondent, and the point concerns what they know about other networks.
questions.trap: Assuming weak ties are valuable because of power or trust, not because of their position in different networks.

questions.stem: Of all the new leads reported in Table 1, approximately what percentage came through weak ties?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) New leads: strong = 0.20 x 100 = 20; weak = 0.60 x 150 = 90. Weak share = 90 / 110, about 82%. Why the others are wrong: B) 60% is the weak-tie rate of new leads within weak ties, not the share of all new leads. C) 36% is 90 / 250, the proportion of all hires who got a new lead through a weak tie. D) 18% is 20 / 110, the strong-tie share of new leads.
questions.trap: Using the within-group percentage (60%) as if it were the share of all new leads.

questions.stem: About how many times more likely was a given strong tie than a given weak tie to produce a hire?

options.A: About 0.7 times
options.B: About 6.7 times
options.C: About 10 times
options.D: About 1.5 times

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Per respondent, 12 strong ties yielded 100/400 hires on average and 120 weak ties yielded 150/400; per tie, 100/(400 x 12) is about 2.1% versus 150/(400 x 120), about 0.31%, a ratio of about 6.7. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.67 is 100 / 150, the ratio of total hires without adjusting for number of ties. C) 10 is the ratio of the numbers of weak to strong ties, not of hire rates per tie. D) 1.5 is 150 / 100, which compares total hires and ignores the number of ties.
questions.trap: Comparing raw hire counts and ignoring that respondents had ten times as many weak ties to draw from.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of surveying only workers who had recently found jobs?

options.A: The workers cannot report how frequently they see each contact, so tie strength cannot be determined.
options.B: It cannot show how often each tie type failed to produce a job for unsuccessful searchers.
options.C: The survey includes workers who used advertisements, which makes the contact-based sample too large.
options.D: Workers who changed jobs recently cannot report how many ties they have, so tie counts are unreliable.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Sampling on a successful outcome omits unsuccessful searches, so the effectiveness of each tie type is not fully estimable. Why the others are wrong: A) Respondents can report frequency of contact, and the study coded tie type from it. C) The 250 contact-based hires were analyzed separately, so advertisement users do not inflate the sample. D) Counting ties is a self-report issue but not the main design limitation described.
questions.trap: Focusing on measurement details rather than the sampling-on-outcome problem that limits the conclusions.

questions.stem: Who would most likely benefit from activating weak ties?

options.A: A widow who needs emotional comfort and practical help in the weeks after a loss.
options.B: A graduate seeking openings in an industry where no close friend works.
options.C: A manager who needs to coordinate daily work with colleagues on her own team.
options.D: A student who wants a trusted friend to lend him money during a financial emergency.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Information from outside one's own circle is the main strength of weak ties. Why the others are wrong: A) Emotional support and practical care are typically provided by strong ties. C) Daily coordination relies on frequent, dense contact within the team. D) Trust and willingness to lend money are characteristic of strong ties.
questions.trap: Choosing a scenario involving support or trust rather than access to new information.

passages.passage_text: Demographers compare age structures to anticipate social needs. Table 1 gives population (in millions) by broad age group for Country J in 1990 and 2020 and for Country K in 2020. Estimates come from national censuses adjusted for undercount. The total dependency ratio is the number of people aged 0 to 14 plus those aged 65 and older, per 100 people aged 15 to 64. Both countries have low death rates, and Country J had little net migration over the period. Figure 1 plots the total fertility rate (TFR, the average number of births per woman) for both countries; replacement-level fertility in low-mortality countries is about 2.1. Country K is a lower-middle-income country with a growing urban population and expanding school enrollment, whereas Country J is a high-income country with universal pension coverage financed by taxes on current workers. Ages were grouped by completed years at the census date, and all figures are rounded to the nearest million.

questions.stem: What was the total dependency ratio of Country J in 2020?

options.A: About 36 per 100
options.B: About 38 per 100
options.C: About 19 per 100
options.D: About 56 per 100

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Dependents = 15 + 30 = 45 and working-age = 80, so 45 / 80 = 0.5625, or about 56 per 100. Why the others are wrong: A) 45 / 125 is about 36, which divides by the total population instead of the working-age group. B) 30 / 80 is about 38, which counts only the older dependents. C) 15 / 80 is about 19, which counts only the child dependents.
questions.trap: Dividing dependents by the total population or counting only one dependent group instead of using the working-age group as the denominator.

questions.stem: Between 1990 and 2020, the total population of Country J grew from 110 million to 125 million. Which statement is supported by Table 1?

options.A: Growth in the 65+ group (18 million) exceeded net population growth (15 million).
options.B: The working-age group accounted for most of the net growth in the population over the 30 years.
options.C: Increases in the number of children were the main source of growth during the 30 years.
options.D: The population aged 65 and older grew more slowly than the population aged 0 to 14.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The 65+ group rose from 12 to 30 (+18), the 0-14 group fell by 3, and the 15-64 group was unchanged, so older adults more than account for net growth. Why the others are wrong: B) The 15-64 group stayed at 80 million, so it contributed none of the growth. C) The 0-14 group shrank from 18 to 15 million. D) The 65+ group grew by 150%, while the 0-14 group declined.
questions.trap: Assuming that population growth must come from births rather than from longevity.

questions.stem: Country J's TFR in Figure 1 has been below replacement level for decades. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Without immigration or further gains in longevity, Country J's population would eventually shrink because births fall short of what is needed to replace parents.
options.B: Country J's population must already be declining, because a TFR below 2.1 immediately lowers the total population.
options.C: Below-replacement fertility cannot affect the age structure unless death rates also rise sharply.
options.D: Country J's falling TFR shows that it has not completed the demographic transition.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Below-replacement fertility leads to eventual decline, but momentum and longer life spans can keep the total from falling for years. Why the others are wrong: B) Population momentum and longevity delay decline; J actually grew from 110 to 125 million. C) Persistently low fertility changes age structure on its own, producing an older population. D) Low births and low deaths describe a completed transition; low TFR is consistent with it.
questions.trap: Equating a below-replacement TFR with immediate population decline and forgetting about momentum and longevity.

questions.stem: Which stage of demographic transition best describes Country K in 2020?

options.A: Stage 1, with high birth rates and high death rates that keep growth near zero
options.B: Stage 3, with falling fertility that is still well above replacement
options.C: Stage 4, with low birth rates and low death rates and a roughly stable population
options.D: A post-transition stage with fertility far below replacement and an aging population

questions.explanation: Correct: B) K has few older adults, a large child population, a TFR of 3.9 and declining, and low mortality, which matches the late stage 2 to stage 3 pattern in which growth is still substantial. Why the others are wrong: A) High death rates are inconsistent with the stated low mortality in K. C) A TFR of 3.9 is far above the near-replacement level that characterizes stage 4. D) J, not K, fits the description with TFR 1.3 and an older population.
questions.trap: Matching a country to a stage by its falling fertility alone, without checking how far it is above replacement.

questions.stem: How did the number of working-age people per person aged 65 and older in Country J change from 1990 to 2020?

options.A: It rose from 15 to 38.
options.B: It fell from 12 to 30.
options.C: It fell from about 4.5 to about 2.7.
options.D: It fell from about 6.7 to about 2.7.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) In 1990, 80 / 12 is about 6.7; in 2020, 80 / 30 is about 2.7, so fewer workers support each older person. Why the others are wrong: A) 15 and 38 are the old-age dependency ratios (65+ per 100 working-age), which rose, not workers per older person. B) 12 and 30 are the raw counts of older people, which rose. C) 4.5 does not match 80 / 12, and the 1990 value was about 6.7.
questions.trap: Reporting the old-age dependency ratio, which rose, when the question asks for its reciprocal, which fell.

passages.passage_text: Researchers surveyed 2,000 households in one metropolitan area to compare income, wealth (assets minus debts), and homeownership between two social groups, labeled Group P and Group Q, which have differed historically in access to credit and housing. Table 1 reports medians for all households and for households headed by a college graduate. Data were collected at a single time point. Researchers reported medians rather than means, and noted that Group Q households were more likely to be renters in neighborhoods where property values have risen slowly, whereas Group P households were more likely to own homes in neighborhoods where values have risen quickly. Households were sampled at random from tax and housing records, interviews were conducted in person, and wealth was reported for the previous calendar year. Respondents who declined to report an asset value were excluded from the wealth calculations. Income was reported before taxes, and households were classified by the group of the person who owned or rented the home.
passages.table_data:
| Households | Group | Median income ($) | Median wealth ($) | Homeowners (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All | P | 68,000 | 190,000 | 74 |
| All | Q | 52,000 | 24,000 | 46 |
| College graduates | P | 98,000 | 310,000 | 85 |
| College graduates | Q | 79,000 | 61,000 | 63 |

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the gaps for all households in Table 1?

options.A: The ratio of Group P to Group Q was about 1.3 for median income but about 7.9 for median wealth.
options.B: The ratio of Group P to Group Q was about 7.9 for median income but about 1.3 for median wealth.
options.C: The ratios of Group P to Group Q were nearly identical for median income and median wealth.
options.D: Group Q had a higher homeownership rate than Group P but a lower median wealth.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) 68,000 / 52,000 is about 1.3, and 190,000 / 24,000 is about 7.9, so the wealth gap is much wider than the income gap. Why the others are wrong: B) The ratios are reversed in this option. C) A 1.3 ratio and a 7.9 ratio are far from identical. D) Group P's homeownership (74%) was higher than Group Q's (46%).
questions.trap: Reading a modest income gap as evidence of a similarly modest wealth gap.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains why the wealth gap is wider than the income gap?

options.A: Wealth is calculated only from annual earnings, so any gap in income is automatically magnified in wealth.
options.B: Households in the lower-wealth group save a smaller fraction of every dollar of income than households in the other group.
options.C: Wealth is measured at the individual level, while income is measured at the household level.
options.D: Wealth accumulates over time and across generations through assets such as home equity and inheritance, whereas income is a yearly flow.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Historical differences in credit and housing access produce cumulative advantage or disadvantage that shows up more strongly in assets than in income. Why the others are wrong: A) Wealth is assets minus debts, not a function of earnings alone. B) Nothing in the table shows saving rates differ; the passage points to housing and credit access. C) Both measures here are reported at the household level.
questions.trap: Attributing the gap to individual choices when structural, cumulative factors are described in the passage.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about education is supported by Table 1?

options.A: College education eliminated the wealth gap between the two groups.
options.B: College-educated Group Q households held about one-fifth the median wealth of college-educated Group P households.
options.C: College-educated Group Q households owned homes at a higher rate than all Group P households.
options.D: College-educated households in both groups had lower median incomes than non-college households.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) 61,000 / 310,000 is about 0.20, so a large wealth gap remained at the same education level. Why the others are wrong: A) A gap of $249,000 in median wealth between college graduates is not eliminated. C) Group Q college graduates owned homes at 63%, below the 74% rate for all Group P households. D) Median incomes were higher for college graduates in both groups (98,000 and 79,000 versus 68,000 and 52,000).
questions.trap: Assuming equal educational attainment should equalize wealth.

questions.stem: Why did the researchers report medians rather than means for wealth?

options.A: A few extremely wealthy households would pull the mean far above what a typical household holds.
options.B: Medians can be calculated even when some households did not report their wealth, whereas means cannot.
options.C: Medians are less affected by the number of households and therefore needed no measure of sample size.
options.D: Wealth is a categorical variable, and only medians can be computed for categorical data.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Wealth distributions are strongly right-skewed, so the median better represents a typical household. Why the others are wrong: B) Missing data affect both statistics; this is not why medians are preferred. C) Sample size still matters for any statistic. D) Wealth is a continuous variable, not a categorical one.
questions.trap: Believing the choice of median is about missing data or variable type rather than skewness.

passages.passage_text: Researchers developed an 8-item Brief Loneliness Scale (BLS; scores range from 8 to 40, higher scores indicating greater loneliness) and administered it to 150 adults. Internal consistency was assessed with Cronbach's alpha. A subgroup of 60 adults completed the BLS again two weeks later, during which no major life events were reported. All 150 adults also completed an established 20-item loneliness measure, an extraversion measure, and a social desirability measure (tendency to answer so as to look good). Table 1 summarizes the statistics. Figure 1 plots first and second BLS scores for 12 participants selected at random from the retest subgroup. The adults were recruited from community centers and online notices and were paid a small fee for each session. Items such as 'I feel left out' were rated for frequency over the past month, from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Higher scores on the established measure also indicate greater loneliness.
passages.table_data:
| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Cronbach's alpha (n = 150) | 0.88 |
| Test-retest correlation, 2 weeks (n = 60) | 0.81 |
| Correlation with established loneliness measure | 0.74 |
| Correlation with extraversion | -0.35 |
| Correlation with social desirability | 0.05 |

graph.title: Figure 1. BLS scores at first and second administration (12 participants)

questions.stem: What does a Cronbach's alpha of 0.88 indicate about the BLS?

options.A: The scale measures loneliness and not some other construct.
options.B: Participants' scores remain stable over a two-week interval.
options.C: The items tend to vary together, indicating good internal consistency.
options.D: The scale predicts later social isolation better than other measures do.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Alpha summarizes how strongly items correlate with each other, an index of internal-consistency reliability. Why the others are wrong: A) That describes validity, which alpha does not establish. B) Stability over time is test-retest reliability, reported separately as 0.81. D) Predictive power is a validity question that is not addressed here.
questions.trap: Treating a reliability coefficient as evidence that the scale measures the intended construct.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of the variance in BLS scores is shared with the established loneliness measure?
questions.explanation: Correct: A) The coefficient of determination is r squared: 0.74 x 0.74 is about 0.55. Why the others are wrong: B) 0.74 is the correlation coefficient itself, not the shared variance. C) 0.86 is the square root of 0.74, which is an incorrect transformation. D) 0.45 is the unshared variance (1 - 0.55).
questions.trap: Reporting r as if it were the proportion of variance explained.

questions.stem: What does the correlation of 0.05 with social desirability suggest?

options.A: The BLS is highly reliable because it does not depend on social desirability.
options.B: Participants who are more socially desirable are unlikely to be lonely.
options.C: Responses on the BLS are not strongly influenced by a tendency to look good, supporting discriminant validity.
options.D: The BLS measures extraversion rather than loneliness.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A scale should correlate weakly with constructs it is not meant to measure; 0.05 indicates little overlap with social desirability. Why the others are wrong: A) Low correlation with an unrelated measure is evidence of validity, not reliability. B) A near-zero correlation says there is essentially no relationship, not a negative one. D) The correlation with extraversion is moderate (-0.35), but it does not show the BLS measures extraversion.
questions.trap: Confusing discriminant validity with reliability.

questions.stem: Suppose every participant's BLS score at the second testing was exactly 3 points lower than at the first. What would happen to the test-retest correlation?

options.A: It would fall, because the scores would no longer be the same on both occasions.
options.B: It would be unchanged, since correlation reflects relative standing.
options.C: It would become negative, because scores moved in the opposite direction.
options.D: It would rise to 1.0 only if the scores also became more spread out.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Adding or subtracting a constant shifts all scores equally and leaves their relative ordering and the correlation unchanged. Why the others are wrong: A) Correlation does not require equal scores, only a consistent linear relationship. C) A uniform decrease still ranks participants the same way, so the correlation does not turn negative. D) Changing spread alone would not change the correlation either.
questions.trap: Assuming that a correlation measures agreement of exact scores rather than similarity in rank order.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the BLS is best supported by Table 1 and Figure 1?

options.A: The BLS has been shown to measure loneliness without error because its correlations are all strong.
options.B: Scores were stable, but that does not prove the BLS measures loneliness.
options.C: Participants' scores did not change at all between the two administrations.
options.D: A correlation of -0.35 with extraversion shows that low extraversion causes loneliness.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A retest r of 0.81 means good stability, whereas validity needs evidence like the correlation with an established measure. Why the others are wrong: A) Not all correlations are strong, and no scale is error-free. C) The scatter plot shows individual score changes between times, so scores did vary. D) A correlation cannot establish causal direction.
questions.trap: Equating reliability with validity or reading a correlation as causal.

passages.passage_text: A new blood test screens for a disease. Researchers applied the test and a definitive diagnostic procedure to 1,000 adults from a clinic where 10% of patients have the disease. A test result was positive if the biomarker concentration exceeded 40 units/mL. Table 1 gives the results. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative, and positive predictive value (PPV) is the proportion of positive results that are true positives. Researchers are also considering using the test for population screening in a community where disease prevalence is 1%, and 10,000 adults would be tested. Assume that sensitivity and specificity are the same as in the clinic. The clinic sample was drawn at random from consecutive patients who came for evaluation of symptoms, and the people who performed the diagnostic procedure did not know the blood test results.
passages.table_data:
| Test result | Disease present | Disease absent |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | 90 | 90 |
| Negative | 10 | 810 |

questions.stem: What is the sensitivity of the test in the clinic sample?
questions.explanation: Correct: D) Sensitivity = true positives / all with disease = 90 / 100 = 90%. Why the others are wrong: A) 50% is the PPV (90 / 180), not sensitivity. B) 99% is not obtainable from the table; 810 / 820 is the negative predictive value, about 98.8%. C) 10% is the proportion of those with the disease who test negative (false negatives).
questions.trap: Using the positive result column as the denominator, which gives PPV rather than sensitivity.

questions.stem: What is the PPV of the test in the clinic sample?
questions.explanation: Correct: B) PPV = 90 true positives / 180 positive results = 50%. Why the others are wrong: A) 90% is sensitivity and specificity, not PPV. C) 10% is the prevalence in the clinic sample. D) 90.9% does not follow from the table.
questions.trap: Confusing PPV with sensitivity because the number 90 appears in both calculations.

questions.stem: In the 10,000-person community screening scenario, what would the PPV be?

options.A: About 50%
options.B: About 90%
options.C: About 1%
options.D: About 8%

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Disease present = 100, of whom 90 test positive; disease absent = 9,900, of whom 10% (990) test positive. PPV = 90 / (90 + 990), about 8%. Why the others are wrong: A) 50% is the clinic value, which depends on 10% prevalence. B) 90% is the sensitivity and does not equal PPV. C) 1% is the prevalence, not the PPV.
questions.trap: Carrying the clinic PPV over to a population with a different prevalence.

questions.stem: Why is the PPV lower when the same test is used in a lower-prevalence population?

options.A: False positives from the large disease-free group outnumber true positives from the small affected group.
options.B: The test's sensitivity falls when fewer people in the sample have the disease.
options.C: The specificity of the test increases, which reduces the number of correct positive results.
options.D: Fewer people agree to testing in low-prevalence communities, which lowers the number of true positives.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) PPV depends on prevalence; with a rare disease, even a small false-positive rate yields many false positives relative to true cases. Why the others are wrong: B) Sensitivity is a property of the test given the disease and does not change with prevalence. C) Specificity stays the same by assumption, and a higher specificity would raise PPV. D) Participation rates are not part of the PPV calculation.
questions.trap: Thinking that prevalence changes the test's sensitivity or specificity instead of the predictive values.

questions.stem: If researchers lowered the positivity cutoff from 40 to 25 units/mL, what would most likely happen?

options.A: Both sensitivity and specificity would increase.
options.B: Sensitivity would decrease and specificity would increase.
options.C: Sensitivity would increase and specificity would decrease.
options.D: Both sensitivity and specificity would decrease.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A lower threshold labels more people positive, catching more true cases but also more healthy people. Why the others are wrong: A) Both cannot improve by shifting a single cutoff when the distributions overlap. B) This describes raising the cutoff rather than lowering it. D) Moving a single cutoff trades one for the other, not a decline in both.
questions.trap: Forgetting that the two accuracy measures trade off with the cutoff.

discrete.stem: A participant can just barely tell the difference between a 100 g weight and a 102 g weight. If Weber's law holds, what is the smallest difference likely to be noticed when the standard is 300 g?

options.A: 6 g
options.B: 2 g
options.C: 3 g

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) The Weber fraction is 2 / 100 = 0.02, so for a 300 g standard the just noticeable difference is 0.02 x 300 = 6 g. Why the others are wrong: B) 2 g would hold the absolute difference constant, which Weber's law does not predict. C) 3 g is not obtained from a constant proportion of the larger standard. D) 12 g doubles the correct value.
discrete.trap: Keeping the absolute difference (2 g) constant instead of the proportion.

discrete.stem: A listener hears a high-pitched tone. According to place theory, which part of the basilar membrane is maximally displaced?

options.A: The region near the apex, at the far end of the cochlea
options.B: The middle region, which responds equally to all frequencies
options.C: The region near the base, close to the oval window
options.D: The tympanic membrane, which vibrates at the frequency of the tone

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) In the cochlea, the base is narrow and stiff and responds to high frequencies, while the apex responds to low frequencies. Why the others are wrong: A) The apex is tuned to low frequencies. B) No region responds equally to all frequencies; tuning is tonotopic. D) The tympanic membrane is in the middle ear and is not part of the basilar membrane.
discrete.trap: Reversing the frequency map of the cochlea.

discrete.stem: A person remembers the ten-digit number 5558675309 more easily by thinking of it as 555, 867, and 5309. This strategy is an example of:

options.A: maintenance rehearsal
options.B: chunking
options.C: the serial position effect
options.D: the method of loci

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Chunking groups items into larger meaningful units, increasing how much working memory can hold. Why the others are wrong: A) Maintenance rehearsal is repeating items without reorganizing them. C) The serial position effect is better recall of items at the start and end of a list. D) The method of loci links items to places along a mental route.
discrete.trap: Choosing a memory strategy by name recognition rather than by what the person actually did to the digits.

discrete.stem: A patient speaks slowly and with great effort, using mostly content words, but understands spoken questions and follows commands well. Damage to which area is most likely?

options.A: Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
options.B: Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
options.C: The arcuate fasciculus connecting the language areas
options.D: The primary auditory cortex in both hemispheres

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Nonfluent speech with relatively intact comprehension is characteristic of damage to Broca's area, which is involved in speech production. Why the others are wrong: B) Wernicke's damage causes fluent, meaningless speech with poor comprehension. C) Arcuate damage mainly impairs repetition while leaving comprehension and fluency intact. D) Bilateral auditory damage would impair comprehension, not just production.
discrete.trap: Associating any language deficit with Wernicke's area.

discrete.stem: After a week of news coverage of a rare disease, a woman estimates that the disease is far more common than statistics indicate. This is best explained by:

options.A: the representativeness heuristic
options.B: functional fixedness
options.C: the availability heuristic
options.D: belief perseverance

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) People judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind, and heavy coverage makes examples vivid and accessible. Why the others are wrong: A) Representativeness involves judging by similarity to a prototype, not ease of recall. B) Functional fixedness is a limit on using objects in new ways. D) Belief perseverance is holding a belief despite disconfirming evidence.
discrete.trap: Mistaking a frequency judgment based on ease of recall for a judgment based on similarity.

discrete.stem: A man's heart begins pounding when he sees a snake on the trail. He concludes that he is afraid because his heart is pounding. Which theory does this sequence best illustrate?

options.A: Cannon-Bard theory
options.B: Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
options.C: James-Lange theory
options.D: Opponent-process theory

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) James-Lange holds that the experience of emotion follows from perceiving bodily arousal. Why the others are wrong: A) Cannon-Bard says arousal and emotion occur simultaneously and independently. B) Two-factor theory requires cognitive labeling of arousal using situational cues. D) Opponent-process theory concerns the hedonic aftereffects of emotional or drug states.
discrete.trap: Picking the better-known two-factor theory without checking whether the cognitive labeling step is described.

discrete.stem: According to the Yerkes-Dodson law, which level of arousal is most likely to produce the best performance on a very complex, unfamiliar task?

options.A: High arousal
options.B: Arousal that is as high as possible on every task
options.C: No arousal at all
options.D: Low to moderate arousal

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) The optimal arousal level is lower for difficult tasks and higher for simple or well-learned tasks. Why the others are wrong: A) High arousal helps simple tasks but tends to impair complex ones. B) More arousal does not always improve performance, since the relation is an inverted U. C) Some arousal is needed for alertness; zero arousal would impair performance.
discrete.trap: Assuming more motivation always improves performance.

discrete.stem: In a study of twins, the correlation for a trait is 0.80 for monozygotic pairs and 0.45 for dizygotic pairs. Using Falconer's formula, the estimated heritability is:
discrete.explanation: Correct: C) Heritability is estimated as 2 x (rMZ - rDZ) = 2 x 0.35 = 0.70. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.35 is the difference in correlations without doubling. B) 0.45 is the DZ correlation, not an estimate of heritability. D) 0.80 is the MZ correlation, which includes shared environment as well as genes.
discrete.trap: Using the difference in correlations without doubling it.

discrete.stem: A man who harbors intense, unacceptable hostility toward his coworker becomes unusually warm and solicitous toward that coworker. Which Freudian defense mechanism best explains this behavior?

options.A: Projection, attributing his own hostility to the coworker
options.B: Reaction formation, acting opposite to the impulse
options.C: Displacement, redirecting the hostility toward a safer target
options.D: Sublimation, channeling the hostility into a socially valued activity

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite, so hostility appears as exaggerated friendliness. Why the others are wrong: A) Projection would lead him to believe the coworker is hostile toward him, not to act warmly. C) Displacement would direct the hostility toward a less threatening person or object, but here it is not expressed at all. D) Sublimation would channel the impulse into a constructive outlet such as sport or art, not into its opposite emotion.
discrete.trap: Choosing displacement or sublimation because the hostility is being redirected, when the behavior is the direct opposite of the impulse.

discrete.stem: A researcher runs 20 independent hypothesis tests at alpha = 0.05 when all null hypotheses are true. About how many statistically significant results should be expected by chance alone?
discrete.explanation: Correct: D) The expected number of false positives is 20 x 0.05 = 1, which is why multiple comparisons require correction. Why the others are wrong: A) Zero would require no Type I errors at all, which alpha = 0.05 does not guarantee. B) Five would correspond to a 25% error rate per test. C) Twenty would mean every test came out significant.
discrete.trap: Ignoring that the Type I error rate applies to each test independently.

discrete.stem: A random sample of 100 adults has a mean systolic blood pressure of 120 mm Hg with a standard deviation of 10 mm Hg. Which interval is the best approximation of the 95% confidence interval for the population mean?

options.A: 118 to 122 mm Hg
options.B: 100 to 140 mm Hg
options.C: 110 to 130 mm Hg
options.D: 119 to 121 mm Hg

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) SE = 10 / 10 = 1, and the interval is roughly the mean plus or minus 2 SE, 118 to 122. Why the others are wrong: B) 100 to 140 is the mean plus or minus 2 SD, which describes the spread of individuals. C) 110 to 130 is plus or minus 1 SD. D) 119 to 121 is plus or minus 1 SE, a roughly 68% interval.
discrete.trap: Using the standard deviation instead of the standard error.

discrete.stem: A hospital study finds that patients taking vitamin D supplements have more bone fractures than those who do not. Which explanation is most plausible?

options.A: Vitamin D supplements directly weaken bones in all patients who take them.
options.B: The result must be due to chance, because observational studies cannot detect real associations.
options.C: Patients who do not take supplements are less likely to be admitted to the hospital.
options.D: Patients at higher risk of fractures, such as those with weak bones, were more likely to be prescribed the supplement.

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) Reverse causation or confounding by indication: the outcome risk may have led to the treatment. Why the others are wrong: A) A direct harm cannot be concluded from observational association alone. B) Observational studies can detect real associations; they just cannot establish causation. C) Nothing in the stem suggests unequal admission rates.
discrete.trap: Reading an association in observational data as evidence that the treatment caused the outcome.
